sections.title: What to include on a photography invoice
sections.body: A professional photography invoice does more than ask for money. It acts as a record of the shoot and defines what the client is actually buying. You must clearly separate your creative fee from the usage license. The client needs to see exactly what they are paying for your time on set versus their right to publish the images. You also need to detail any hard costs incurred during the production. Using our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator lets you structure these line items instantly without creating an account.
items: Shoot fees billed as half-day or full-day rates
Specific licensing terms and usage durations
Crew costs for second shooters and lighting assistants
Travel expenses including mileage and per diem

sections.title: Billing for production, crew, and post-processing
sections.body: Photography billing is rarely a single flat fee. Most commercial and editorial photographers break their pricing into distinct phases. First is the production phase, which covers your time, equipment, and crew. Second is post-production, where you bill for editing, colour grading, and retouching per image. Finally, there are the expenses. If a shoot requires specific props, studio rentals, or travel, these are passed directly to the client. Breaking these costs down prevents clients from questioning the total and helps them understand the true cost of a professional production.
items: Charge a distinct fee for your time on set
Bill editing and retouching on a per-image basis
Pass through costs for studio hire and equipment rental
Itemise travel costs like flights and hotel stays

sections.title: Deposits, payment terms, and image delivery
sections.body: Cash flow is a common challenge for freelance photographers. To protect yourself, always require a non-refundable booking fee or deposit before confirming a shoot date. This covers your initial prep time and secures the calendar slot. For the final balance, the best protection you have is the work itself. Standard practice is to provide low-resolution watermarked proofs for selection, but withhold the final high-resolution files until the invoice is paid in full. State this policy clearly in your payment terms on every document you send.
items: Require a deposit to secure the shoot date
State your payment terms clearly on the invoice
Tie the delivery of high-resolution files to final payment
Send clear payment reminders for overdue balances

faqs.q: Should I charge a half-day or full-day rate?
faqs.a: Most professional photographers avoid hourly billing for shoots. A half-day rate typically covers up to four hours, while a full-day rate covers up to eight. This structure accounts for the reality that a short shoot still requires packing gear, travelling, setting up, and breaking down, which often ruins the chance to book a second job that same day.

faqs.q: How do I bill for a second shooter or assistant?
faqs.a: Crew costs should be listed as separate line items on your invoice. If you hire a second shooter, a lighting assistant, or a digital tech, bill their day rates directly to the client. You can choose to add a small markup to cover your administrative time in sourcing and managing the crew, but the cost must be transparent.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a shoot fee and a licensing fee?
faqs.a: A shoot fee, or creative fee, pays for your time, skill, and equipment on the day of the production. A licensing fee pays for the client's right to use the resulting images. Licensing costs vary wildly depending on where the images will be used, for how long, and the size of the audience.

faqs.q: How should I handle travel expenses and per diems?
faqs.a: When a shoot requires travel, bill the client for your mileage, flights, and accommodation. A per diem is a set daily allowance to cover your meals and incidental expenses while away from home. List these clearly on your invoice so the client knows exactly what portion of the bill covers your hard costs rather than your profit.
